title: What not to fix when selling a house: The ROI matrix, deal-breakers, and smarter repair credits
summary: Which pre-sale repairs pay off and which to skip, based on NAR cost-recovery data: curb appeal, paint and entry doors lead; kitchen remodels and pools trail.
body_markdown:
*By Otto Acosta, Offerpad Research Team*


Putting a property on the market and expecting a quick sale is what many owners want, but focusing on speed may come at the expense of achieving the desired price in all but the most competitive of real estate markets. Most homes require some degree of repair work to attract the right buyers and attain an optimal asking price. Sellers should focus on return on investment (ROI) for any work undertaken.


Data from the National Association of Realtors (NAR) and other industry bodies provides specific insights into the aspects of a home that should be the focus of pre-sale repair spending, as well as those areas that have the least impact on salability and the worst ROI.


## Addressing the Buyer Expectation Disconnect


An important finding to focus on first and foremost comes from[NAR research into home staging](https://www.nar.realtor/news/real-estate-news/staging-to-sell-the-real-estate-shift-toward-picture-perfect-homes) , meaning the process by which agents and their clients prepare properties for sale by preparing interior spaces in a way that’s most appealing to prospective buyers. Fifty-eight percent of professionals in the industry said that buyer disappointment stemmed most frequently from the gap between how homes appear in promotional images and how they look during an in-person visit.


Almost three-quarters said real estate shows on TV were to blame for much of this disconnect. In turn, a properly staged home can increase a home’s sale price by as much as 10% in the best cases. Meanwhile, time on market for a properly staged property can drop as well, with 49% of agents saying that it either slightly or greatly reduced the period between a listing going live and an offer being made.


According to[Offerpad](https://www.offerpad.com/) , a real estate technology company, the counterintuitive conclusion to draw from this data is that the most affordable and superficial changes can deliver the greatest ROI in terms of sale price and buyer interest. The rise of virtual staging and the relatively recent introduction of AI-powered image generation to enable agents to create visualizations of what a home could look like once renovated as a means of attracting buyers further cements the importance of this finding.


Staging costs vary, with agents able to handle it themselves for $500, while professionals in the field charge $1,500 on average. In either case, it’s a modest fee in the context of the average home sale price, with the median[currently sitting at $410,700](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MSPUS) .


## Choosing Repairs According to Cost Recovery


Despite the obvious impact that simple staging has on house salability and sales price, there are many properties that require more hands-on work to bring them up to scratch to align with market expectations and bring in buyers with attractive offers in tow. The NAR’s[2025 Remodeling Impact Report](https://www.nar.realtor/press-releases/top-remodeling-projects-for-homeowner-satisfaction-and-cost-recovery-revealed-in-nar-report) provides clear insights into exactly where owners should focus their efforts if they want optimal ROI.


When deciding where to allocate pre-sale capital, industry cost-recovery data reveals these priorities:


### The Presale ROI Cheat Sheet


- **High ROI (Prioritize):** Standard lawn care (217%), landscape maintenance (104%), steel entry door replacement (100%), and interior paint touch-ups.
- **Low ROI (Skip):** Full kitchen remodels (60%), in-ground pools (56%), primary bedroom additions (54%), and luxury outdoor fire pits.


There’s a difference between what homeowners might want to do to improve their property and what industry professionals feel adds the most value when it’s time to sell. While personal preference often drives home improvements, emotional satisfaction rarely aligns with direct financial return. The NAR’s research highlights a distinct gap between the projects that bring homeowners the most joy and those that actually recover their costs at resale.


For example, adding a primary bedroom suite or executing a complete kitchen overhaul both score a perfect 10 out of 10 on the NAR Joy Score index. However, when it comes to financial returns, a complete kitchen renovation recovers only[60% of its cost](https://www.nar.realtor/news/styled-staged-sold/home-upgrades-that-can-pay-off-at-resale) , and a full primary suite addition recoups just 54%. In contrast, simple utility-focused updates deliver the highest cost recovery.


Installing a new steel front door yields a 100% cost recovery at resale, while a closet renovation recaptures roughly 83% of the initial outlay. Rather than sinking capital into extensive gut renovations, real estate agents overwhelmingly suggest focused, cost-effective prep work. Half of all agents (50%) recommend painting the entire interior before listing and 41% suggest painting a single room. Directing funds toward high-yielding functional touch-ups prevents equity from getting trapped in major overhauls.


## Outdoor ROI versus High-Cost Backyard Traps


Data from the[NAR Remodeling Impact Report: Outdoor Features](https://www.nar.realtor/research-and-statistics/research-reports/remodeling-impact-report-outdoor-features) shows that exterior curb appeal delivers some of the highest financial returns in real estate. Basic lawn care services yield 217% cost recovery, making standard turf maintenance the most profitable pre-sale exterior update. General landscape maintenance recaptures 104% of its cost, while an overall landscape upgrade breaks even at 100% ROI.


In contrast, expensive lifestyle features drag down seller proceeds. Adding an in-ground pool costs tens of thousands of dollars but recovers only about 56% of its cost. Outdoor fire features and custom landscape lighting yield similarly low financial returns, hovering around 56% to 59% cost recovery. While these additions boast high Joy Scores among current residents, few agents recommend adding a pool or an outdoor kitchen before listing a property.


## Evaluating Non-Essential Repairs Against Direct Negotiation Credits


Trying to fix every minor defect before opening a property to prospective buyers often creates delays and unexpected expenses. Cosmetic flaws such as outdated cabinet finishes or minor paint chips rarely derail a transaction. Full room gutting often backfires, since buyers usually prefer to customize finishes themselves after purchase.


While superficial cosmetic updates can safely be bypassed, non-negotiable deal-breakers center almost exclusively on lender-mandated habitability requirements, such as active roof leaks, hazardous electrical wiring, and inoperable heating systems, that directly halt buyer mortgage underwriting.


When functional issues arise during inspections, offering closing credits or using modern cash-offer tools lets sellers bypass contractor scheduling bottlenecks. Price concessions keep transactions moving without requiring sellers to manage complex construction tasks right before closing. Direct financial adjustments let buyers address updates on their own timeline while preserving the seller’s immediate cash liquidity.


## An ROI Strategy for Maximum Sale Price


Focusing on high-impact areas delivers superior results over trying to eliminate every flaw. Simple, foundational investments in curb appeal, fresh paint, and clean entryways create immediate buyer interest without draining equity. Sellers who prioritize ROI data over personal preferences consistently secure cleaner transactions and preserve a higher percentage of their final sale price.
